fundamentals.explain: Weight is the force of gravity: W = m × g.

fundamentals.prompt: The unit of force is the…
The unit of energy is the…

fundamentals.explain: p = mv. Velocity, not speed: momentum is a vector.

choices: F is proportional to the rate of change of momentum
fundamentals.explain: Resultant force ∝ rate of change of momentum: F = Δp/Δt.
fundamentals.skill: Force = rate of change of momentum
Force = rate of change of momentum

fundamentals.prompt: Momentum is conserved only if no resultant external force acts.
fundamentals.explain: That's the condition in the conservation principle.

fundamentals.prompt: In an elastic collision, what is conserved?
fundamentals.explain: Elastic: KE conserved too. Momentum is always conserved.

fundamentals.prompt: Elastic: speed of approach = speed of ___
Eₖ in terms of p and m:
A ball of mass m hits a wall at v and rebounds at v. Size of Δp?

fundamentals.explain: KE is a scalar. Momentum is a vector.

fundamentals.prompt: Bouncing ball: in at 5 m s⁻¹, out at 3 m s⁻¹. For Δp, use a speed change of…

steps.title: How fast?
steps.text:
Speed tells you how much distance something covers in a certain time.

speed = distance ÷ time

In physics we measure distance in meters (m) and time in seconds (s), so speed is in meters per second (m/s).

steps.prompt: A runner covers 100 m in 20 s. What is their average speed?
A car drives 150 m in 6 s. What is its average speed?

steps.title: Speed vs. velocity
steps.text:
Velocity is speed with a direction.

"20 m/s" is a speed. "20 m/s north" is a velocity.

Two cars at the same speed going opposite ways have different velocities.

steps.prompt: A car going around a roundabout at a steady 10 m/s has a constant velocity.
steps.explain: Its speed stays the same, but its direction keeps changing, so its velocity changes.

steps.prompt: How far does a cyclist travel in 8 s at a steady 4 m/s?
steps.explain: distance = speed × time = 4 × 8 = 32 m.

steps.title: Speeding up
steps.text:
Acceleration is how quickly velocity changes.

acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time

Its unit is meters per second squared (m/s²): how many m/s you gain every second.

steps.prompt: A bike goes from 0 to 12 m/s in 4 s. What is its acceleration?
A car slows from 20 m/s to 10 m/s in 5 s. What is its acceleration?
steps.explain: (10 − 20) ÷ 5 = −2 m/s². Negative means it is slowing down (in the direction it moves).

steps.title: Falling
steps.text:
Near Earth's surface, things in free fall accelerate downward at about 9.8 m/s², ignoring air resistance.

This is called g.

steps.prompt: Without air resistance, a hammer and a feather dropped together hit the ground at the same time.
steps.explain: Gravity gives every object the same acceleration g. Astronauts showed this on the Moon with a hammer and a feather.

steps.prompt: A rock is dropped from rest. Using g = 9.8 m/s², how fast is it falling after 2 s?

steps.title: Newton's first law
steps.text:
An object keeps doing what it's doing (staying still, or moving at a steady velocity) unless a net force acts on it.

This tendency is called inertia.

steps.prompt: A bus brakes suddenly. Why do standing passengers lurch forward?
choices: Their bodies keep moving forward due to inertia
The air in the bus pushes them
steps.explain: The bus slows, but nothing has slowed the passengers yet, so they keep moving forward.

steps.prompt: A hockey puck sliding on perfectly frictionless ice would eventually stop on its own.
steps.explain: With no friction there is no net force, so it would keep sliding at the same velocity.

steps.title: Net force
steps.text:
Forces have size and direction. The net force is what's left after they combine.

10 N right + 4 N left = 6 N right.

Forces are measured in newtons (N).

steps.prompt: Two people push a box: 30 N to the right and 18 N to the left. What is the net force (in N, to the right)?
steps.explain: 30 − 18 = 12 N to the right.

steps.title: Newton's second law
steps.text:
The net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration.

F = m × a

More force means more acceleration. More mass means less acceleration for the same force.

steps.prompt: What net force accelerates a 2 kg ball at 5 m/s²?
A 40 N net force acts on an 8 kg cart. What is its acceleration?
You push an empty and a full shopping cart with the same force. Which accelerates more?
steps.explain: Same force, less mass → more acceleration.

steps.title: Weight
steps.text:
Weight is the force of gravity on a mass.

W = m × g, with g ≈ 9.8 m/s² on Earth.

Mass (kg) stays the same everywhere; weight (N) depends on gravity.

steps.prompt: What does a 50 kg person weigh on Earth? Use g = 9.8 m/s².

steps.title: Energy of motion
steps.text:
Moving things have kinetic energy.

KE = ½ × m × v²

Energy is measured in joules (J).

steps.prompt: What is the kinetic energy of a 2 kg ball moving at 3 m/s?
If you double a car's speed, its kinetic energy becomes…
steps.explain: KE depends on v². (2v)² = 4v², so the energy is 4× as much. That's why speed matters so much in crashes.

steps.prompt: A parked car has kinetic energy.
steps.explain: v = 0, so KE = 0.

steps.title: Stored by height
steps.text:
Lifting something stores gravitational potential energy.

PE = m × g × h

h is the height in meters.

steps.prompt: How much potential energy does a 3 kg box gain when lifted 2 m? Use g = 9.8 m/s².

steps.title: Energy is conserved
steps.text:
Energy isn't created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another.

As a ball falls, potential energy turns into kinetic energy.

steps.prompt: A ball is dropped from 10 m. Ignoring air resistance, where is its kinetic energy greatest?
choices: Just before it hits the ground
steps.explain: By then almost all its potential energy has turned into kinetic energy.

steps.prompt: On a frictionless track, a roller coaster can never rise higher than the point it started from (at rest).
steps.explain: It can't have more energy than it started with, so it can't gain more height.

steps.prompt: A 0.25 kg ball moves at 12 m s⁻¹. What is its momentum?
A 0.50 kg ball hits a wall at 6.0 m s⁻¹ and rebounds at 4.0 m s⁻¹. Size of its change in momentum?
steps.explain: It bounced, so the speeds add: 0.50 × (6.0 + 4.0) = **5.0 kg m s⁻¹**.
steps.hint: Does the direction change?

steps.prompt: A ball's momentum changes by 0.80 N s in 0.040 s. Average force?
steps.skill: Force = rate of change of momentum

steps.prompt: Water hits a wall at 3.0 kg per second and 12 m s⁻¹, then stops. Force on the wall?
A 1.5 kg trolley at 4.0 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary 0.50 kg trolley. They stick. Common speed?
In an inelastic collision in an isolated system, what is conserved?
steps.explain: Momentum is always conserved. Kinetic energy is not (that's what inelastic means). Total energy is conserved too, but it isn't an option here.

steps.prompt: Elastic collision. A moves right at 8 m s⁻¹, B moves right at 2 m s⁻¹. Afterwards A moves right at 3 m s⁻¹. Velocity of B?
steps.explain:
Approach = 8 − 2 = 6.
Separation: v_B − 3 = 6 → **v_B = 9 m s⁻¹ right**.
steps.hint: Approach speed = separation speed.

steps.prompt: A 0.40 kg puck moves at 3.0 m s⁻¹ in the x-direction and a 0.60 kg puck at 1.0 m s⁻¹ in the y-direction. They stick. Angle to the x-direction?
steps.hint: tan θ = p_y ÷ pₓ

steps.prompt: In an inelastic collision, total energy is lost.
steps.explain: Total energy is always conserved. Only kinetic energy is lost, turning into thermal energy and sound.

steps.prompt: Convert 54 km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹.
On a momentum–time graph, the gradient equals:
steps.explain: Gradient = Δp/Δt = **resultant force**. (The area under an F–t graph is the impulse.)

steps.prompt: A bullet embeds in a hanging block, which then swings up. Which law do you use for the instant the bullet hits?
steps.explain: The bullet sticking in is inelastic, so KE is NOT conserved there. Use **momentum** for the hit, then energy (KE → GPE) for the swing.

steps.title: Momentum = mass × velocity
steps.text:
Momentum is how hard something is to stop.

**p = m × v**

A truck at 10 m s⁻¹ is harder to stop than a bike at 10 m s⁻¹. Same speed, more mass, more momentum.

steps.prompt: A 2 kg ball moves at 3 m s⁻¹. What is its momentum?

steps.title: Units
steps.text:
Unit of momentum: **kg m s⁻¹**

It is the same as **N s** (newton second). Both are correct on a Cambridge paper.

steps.prompt: A 1500 kg car moves at 20 m s⁻¹. What is its momentum?
steps.hint: p = m × v

steps.title: It's a vector
steps.text:
Momentum has a **direction** — the same direction as the velocity.

So it's a **vector**, like velocity and force. Kinetic energy is a **scalar** (no direction).

steps.prompt: Which of these are vectors?
steps.explain: Momentum, velocity and force have direction. Kinetic energy and mass do not.

steps.prompt: Cambridge definition: linear momentum is the product of mass and ___.
steps.explain: Say **velocity**, not speed. Velocity has direction, and so does momentum. Using 'speed' loses the mark.

steps.prompt: 1 N s is the same as 1 kg m s⁻¹.
steps.explain: 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻². Multiply by s: 1 N s = 1 kg m s⁻¹.

steps.prompt: A 0.15 kg ball has momentum 6.0 kg m s⁻¹. What is its speed?
steps.hint: Rearrange p = mv for v.

steps.prompt: Object X has twice the mass and half the speed of object Y. Compare their momenta.
choices: X has four times as much
steps.explain: p_X = (2m)(v/2) = mv = p_Y. **Equal.**

steps.title: Pick a positive direction
steps.text:
Choose one way as **+** (usually right).
Anything going the other way is **−**.

Ball at 4 m s⁻¹ to the right: v = +4
Ball at 4 m s⁻¹ to the left: v = −4

steps.prompt: Right is positive. A 2 kg ball moves LEFT at 5 m s⁻¹. Its momentum is:
steps.explain: p = 2 × (−5) = **−10 kg m s⁻¹**. The minus sign just means 'to the left'.

steps.title: Change in momentum
steps.text:
**Δp = final p − initial p**

Δp = mv − mu

Always **final minus initial**, with signs.

steps.prompt: A 3 kg trolley speeds up from 2 m s⁻¹ to 7 m s⁻¹ (same direction). Find Δp.
steps.hint: Final p minus initial p.

steps.title: The bounce trap
steps.text:
Ball hits a wall at **v** and bounces back at **v**.

Before: +mv
After: −mv
Δp = −mv − (+mv) = **−2mv**

Size of change = **2mv**, NOT zero! The direction flipped, so momentum changed a lot.

steps.prompt: A helium atom of mass m hits a wall at speed v and rebounds along its original path. The collision is perfectly elastic. What is the change in momentum of the atom?
steps.explain:
Before: +mv. After: −mv (same speed, opposite way).
Δp = −mv − mv = −2mv → magnitude **2mv**.

Zero is the trap: speed is the same, but momentum is a vector.

steps.prompt: A 0.20 kg ball hits a wall at 14.0 m s⁻¹ and rebounds at 7.0 m s⁻¹. Size of its change in momentum?
steps.explain:
Take toward wall as +.
Before: 0.20 × 14 = +2.8
After: 0.20 × (−7) = −1.4
Δp = −1.4 − 2.8 = −4.2 → **4.2 kg m s⁻¹**.

When it bounces, the speeds **add** (14 + 7 = 21; 0.20 × 21 = 4.2).
steps.hint: It bounced: does the direction stay the same?

steps.prompt: A ball that bounces back at the same speed has zero change in momentum.
steps.explain: Direction reversed, so Δp = 2mv. Kinetic energy is unchanged, but momentum is not.

steps.prompt: A 60 g ball falls onto the floor at 8.0 m s⁻¹ and bounces up at 6.0 m s⁻¹. Size of the change in momentum?
steps.hint: Convert grams to kg first.

steps.prompt: A ball hits a wall at speed u and sticks (stops). Compared with bouncing back at speed u, the change in momentum is:
steps.explain:
Sticks: Δp = mu.
Bounces: Δp = 2mu.
So sticking gives **half** the change.

lessons.title: Force = rate of change of momentum

steps.title: Newton's 2nd law (Cambridge version)
steps.text:
**The resultant force on an object is proportional to its rate of change of momentum** (and in the same direction).

**F = Δp ÷ Δt**

Memorise that sentence. It's a common definition question.

steps.title: Where F = ma comes from
steps.text:
If the mass stays the same:
F = (mv − mu) ÷ t = m(v − u) ÷ t = **ma**

So F = ma is a special case of F = Δp/Δt.

steps.prompt: Momentum changes by 12 kg m s⁻¹ in 3.0 s. What is the resultant force?
steps.skill: Force = rate of change of momentum
steps.hint: F = Δp ÷ Δt

steps.title: Impulse
steps.text:
**Impulse = F × Δt = Δp**

Impulse is the change in momentum. Same unit: N s.

On a **force–time graph**, impulse = **area under the graph**.

steps.prompt: Force × time is called ___.
steps.explain: Impulse = FΔt, which equals the change in momentum.
steps.skill: Force = rate of change of momentum

steps.prompt: A snooker ball (200 g) hits the cushion at 14.0 m s⁻¹ and rebounds at 7.0 m s⁻¹. Contact time is 0.60 s. Average force from the cushion?
steps.explain:
Δp = 0.200 × (14.0 + 7.0) = 4.2 kg m s⁻¹ (it bounced, so add the speeds).
F = 4.2 ÷ 0.60 = **7.0 N**.

Trap answers: 2.3 N comes from using 14 − 7 instead of 14 + 7.
steps.skill: Force = rate of change of momentum
steps.hint: Find Δp first. It rebounded, so the speeds add.

steps.prompt: A resultant force of 10 N acts on a body for 2.0 s. Which graph could show its momentum p against time t?
steps.explain:
Impulse = 10 × 2.0 = 20 N s, so p must change by **20** in 2.0 s.
A: 20 → ~10 (change 10) ✗
**B: 20 → 0 (change 20) ✓**
C: 10 → 0 ✗   D: 5 → 0 ✗

The force can slow the body down — only the size of the change matters.
steps.alt: Momentum against time graph with four lines A to D
steps.skill: Force = rate of change of momentum
steps.hint: Find the impulse F × t first.

steps.title: Why airbags work
steps.text:
Same Δp, but a **longer Δt** means a **smaller F**.

Airbags, crumple zones and bending your knees when you land all increase the stopping time.

steps.prompt: Why does a crumple zone reduce injuries?
choices: It reduces the change in momentum
It increases the time of the collision, so the force is smaller
It increases the momentum of the car
steps.explain: Δp is fixed (the car still stops). F = Δp/Δt, so a bigger Δt gives a smaller F.
steps.skill: Force = rate of change of momentum

steps.prompt: A glider (1500 kg) starts from rest. The resultant force falls steadily from 10.0 kN to 0 over 40 s. What is its speed when the force reaches zero?
steps.explain:
Impulse = area of the triangle = ½ × 40 × 10 000 = 200 000 N s.
v = Δp ÷ m = 200 000 ÷ 1500 = **133 m s⁻¹**.

Watch the **k** in kN!
steps.alt: Force in kN against time, straight line from 10 kN at 0 s down to 0 at 40 s
steps.skill: Force = rate of change of momentum
steps.hint: Impulse = area under the F–t graph. Watch the kN.

steps.prompt: A 0.045 kg golf ball leaves the club at 60 m s⁻¹. Contact time is 0.50 ms. Average force on the ball?
steps.skill: Force = rate of change of momentum
steps.hint: Convert ms to s.

steps.prompt: State Newton's second law of motion in terms of momentum. Then show that it leads to F = ma when the mass is constant. [3]
steps.solution:
**Law:** the resultant force acting on a body is proportional to the rate of change of its momentum (and acts in the direction of that change).

**Show F = ma:**
F = Δp/Δt = (mv − mu)/t
If m is constant: F = m(v − u)/t
(v − u)/t = a, so **F = ma**.

(With SI units the constant of proportionality is 1.)
steps.skill: Force = rate of change of momentum
steps.hint: Start from F = Δp/Δt and write Δp = mv − mu.

steps.title: Force from a stream
steps.text:
For water, gas, or a stream of pellets:

**F = (mass per second) × (change in velocity)**

F = (Δm/Δt) × Δv

First turn the rate into **kg per second**.

steps.prompt: Convert 90 kg per minute into kg per second.
steps.hint: There are 60 s in a minute.

steps.prompt: Water is pumped through a hose at 90 kg per minute and leaves horizontally at 20 m s⁻¹. What is the minimum force a person must apply to stop the hose moving backwards?
steps.explain:
Mass per second = 90 ÷ 60 = 1.5 kg s⁻¹.
F = 1.5 × 20 = **30 N**.

1800 N comes from forgetting to convert minutes to seconds.

steps.prompt: Steel pellets (0.60 g each) fall onto a plate at 100 pellets per minute. They hit at 5.0 m s⁻¹ and rebound at 4.0 m s⁻¹. Average force on the plate?
steps.explain:
Δp per pellet = 0.00060 × (5.0 + 4.0) = 0.0054 N s (bounce → add speeds).
Pellets per second = 100 ÷ 60 = 1.667.
F = 0.0054 × 1.667 = **0.0090 N**.

0.0054 forgets the rate; 0.0010 subtracts the speeds instead of adding.

steps.prompt: A rocket ejects 25 kg of gas each second at 2000 m s⁻¹ relative to the rocket. What thrust does this give?
steps.hint: Force = (mass per second) × speed.

steps.prompt: A water jet hitting a wall and splashing back produces a bigger force than the same jet stopping dead.
steps.explain: Bouncing back means a bigger Δv (speeds add), so a bigger Δp each second, so a bigger force.

steps.prompt: Rain falls vertically on a flat roof at 0.50 kg per second and hits at 8.0 m s⁻¹, then stops (doesn't bounce). Force on the roof from the rain?
steps.hint: Mass per second × change in velocity.

steps.title: The big rule
steps.text:
**The total momentum of a system stays constant, as long as no resultant external force acts on it.**

Total before = Total after

That's the principle of conservation of momentum. Learn the wording.

steps.title: Why it works
steps.text:
When A pushes B, B pushes A back with an equal and opposite force (Newton's 3rd law), for the same time.

So A gains exactly the momentum B loses. The total doesn't change.

steps.prompt: Momentum is conserved in every collision, as long as the system is isolated.
steps.explain: Elastic, inelastic, sticking, exploding — momentum is always conserved if there's no external resultant force.

steps.title: Recipe
steps.text:
1. Pick + direction.
2. Total p before = add up m × v (with signs).
3. Total p after = same thing.
4. Set equal, solve.

steps.prompt: A 2.0 kg trolley at 3.0 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary 1.0 kg trolley. They stick together. Common speed afterwards?
steps.hint: Total momentum before = total after. They move together.

steps.prompt: A lorry (20 000 kg) moves at 20.0 m s⁻¹ towards a car (900 kg) moving at 30.0 m s⁻¹ towards the lorry. What is the magnitude of the total momentum?
steps.explain:
Lorry +, car − (opposite directions).
20 000 × 20.0 = 400 000
900 × 30.0 = 27 000
Total = 400 000 − 27 000 = 373 000 N s = **373 kN s**.

427 is the trap: adding instead of subtracting.
steps.alt: Lorry moving right at 20 m/s, car moving left at 30 m/s
steps.hint: Opposite directions: one momentum is negative.

steps.prompt: A 20 kg object moving at 6.0 m s⁻¹ collides with a 12 kg object moving at 15 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. They stick together. Speed just after?
steps.explain:
Before: 20 × 6.0 − 12 × 15 = 120 − 180 = −60
After: 32 × v = −60
v = −1.875 → speed **1.9 m s⁻¹** (moving in the 12 kg object's direction).

steps.title: Explosions: start from zero
steps.text:
If everything starts at rest, total momentum = **0**.

After: the pieces fly apart with **equal and opposite** momenta.

m₁v₁ = m₂v₂ (sizes)

The lighter piece goes faster.

steps.prompt: A 4.0 kg gun fires a 0.010 kg bullet at 400 m s⁻¹. Recoil speed of the gun?
steps.explain:
Before: 0.
After: 0.010 × 400 = 4.0 kg m s⁻¹ one way, so the gun has 4.0 the other way.
v = 4.0 ÷ 4.0 = **1.0 m s⁻¹**.
steps.hint: Total momentum before firing is zero.

steps.prompt: Rosetta: an orbiter (170 kg) and lander (100 kg) separate. The lander's velocity changes by 3.0 m s⁻¹ towards the comet. Treat them as isolated. What is the change in speed of the orbiter?
steps.explain:
Work in the frame where they start together (Δ total p = 0).
100 × 3.0 = 170 × Δv
Δv = 300 ÷ 170 = **1.8 m s⁻¹** (away from the comet).
steps.alt: Orbiter 170 kg above, lander 100 kg below moving down at 3.0 m/s
steps.hint: Starts together: the momentum changes are equal and opposite.

steps.prompt: A moving thorium nucleus emits an α-particle and becomes a radium nucleus. Which statement is correct?
choices: The kinetic energy of the α-particle equals that of the radium nucleus.
The momentum of the α-particle equals the momentum of the radium nucleus.
The total momentum before the emission equals the total momentum after.
The velocity of the α-particle equals the velocity of the radium nucleus.
steps.explain:
Isolated system → **total momentum conserved**.
B is wrong here: the thorium was already moving, so the two momenta aren't simply equal (and they're in opposite directions in the picture anyway).
steps.alt: Thorium nucleus moving left; afterwards radium moves left and helium moves right
steps.hint: What is conserved in an isolated system?

steps.prompt: State the principle of conservation of momentum. [2]
steps.solution:
**The total momentum of a system remains constant** (total before = total after) **provided no resultant external force acts on the system.**

Both parts needed for 2 marks: (1) total momentum constant, (2) the condition — isolated / no external resultant force.
steps.hint: Two parts: what stays constant, and when.

steps.title: Two kinds of collision
steps.text:
**Momentum is ALWAYS conserved.**

**Elastic:** kinetic energy is ALSO conserved.
**Inelastic:** some kinetic energy is lost (turned into heat, sound, deformation).

Total **energy** is always conserved. Only **kinetic** energy goes missing.

steps.title: KE reminder
steps.text:
**Eₖ = ½mv²**

KE is a scalar. No minus signs — v² is always positive.

steps.prompt: Kinetic energy of a 4.0 kg object at 3.0 m s⁻¹?
steps.hint: Eₖ = ½mv²

steps.prompt: Two bodies collide and stick together (no external forces). Which is true?
choices: KE the same, momentum the same
steps.explain:
Sticking together = **inelastic**, so KE is lost.
Momentum is always conserved in an isolated system.

steps.prompt: A 4.0 kg object at 3.0 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary object in an inelastic collision. Which statement is correct?
choices: After collision, total KE is 18 J.
After collision, total KE is less than 18 J.
Before collision, total KE is 12 J.
Before collision, total KE is less than 12 J.
steps.explain:
KE before = ½ × 4.0 × 3.0² = 18 J.
Inelastic → some KE is lost → after is **less than 18 J**.

steps.prompt: A body of mass m at velocity v hits a stationary body of the same mass and sticks to it. After the collision, the momentum and KE are:
steps.explain:
Momentum conserved: **mv**.
Speed after: mv = 2m × V → V = v/2.
KE = ½ × 2m × (v/2)² = **¼mv²**.

(Half the KE was lost: it started at ½mv².)

steps.prompt: In a perfectly elastic collision, the total kinetic energy before equals the total kinetic energy after.
steps.explain: That's the definition of elastic.

steps.prompt: Two identical spheres (mass m, speed v) move towards each other and have a head-on elastic collision. Which is correct?
choices: The total kinetic energy after impact is mv².
The total kinetic energy before impact is zero.
The total momentum before impact is 2mv.
steps.explain:
Total momentum = mv − mv = 0 (so D is wrong).
KE is a scalar, it doesn't cancel: ½mv² + ½mv² = mv².
Elastic → KE after = **mv²**.
steps.alt: Two spheres of mass m moving towards each other at speed v
steps.hint: KE is a scalar. Does it cancel?

steps.title: Finding KE lost
steps.text:
1. Use momentum to find the unknown velocity.
2. KE before = sum of ½mv².
3. KE after = sum of ½mv².
4. Loss = before − after.

steps.prompt: A 2.0 kg trolley at 3.0 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary 1.0 kg trolley and they stick (common speed 2.0 m s⁻¹). How much KE is lost?
steps.hint: KE before minus KE after.

steps.prompt: Balls of mass m and 2m move towards each other at 2v and v. After the head-on collision, m rebounds to the left at v. What is the loss of kinetic energy?
steps.explain:
Right = +.
Before: m(2v) + 2m(−v) = 0.
After: m(−v) + 2mV = 0 → V = +v/2.
KE before: ½m(2v)² + ½(2m)v² = 2mv² + mv² = 3mv²
KE after: ½mv² + ½(2m)(v/2)² = ½mv² + ¼mv² = ¾mv²
Loss = 3 − ¾ = **⁹⁄₄ mv²**.
steps.alt: Mass m moving right at 2v towards mass 2m moving left at v
steps.hint: Use momentum to find the 2m ball's velocity first.

steps.prompt: Magnets P and Q on an air track move towards each other and interact without touching. The relative speed of approach equals the relative speed of separation. Which must be correct?
choices: Some of the total KE is lost.
Some of the total momentum is lost.
The momentum of Q after equals the momentum of P before.
The total KE of P and Q before and after are equal.
steps.explain:
Approach speed = separation speed means the collision is **elastic** → total KE is the same before and after.
Momentum is never lost. C only works for special cases (equal masses, Q at rest).
steps.alt: Two magnets P and Q on floats on an air track, moving towards each other
steps.hint: Equal approach and separation speeds means what kind of collision?

steps.title: The shortcut
steps.text:
For a **perfectly elastic** collision in one line:

**speed of approach = speed of separation**

This replaces the messy KE equation. It ONLY works if the collision is elastic.

steps.title: How to get the speeds
steps.text:
**Approach:** how fast the gap closes before.
• Same direction: subtract (20 − 12)
• Towards each other: add (5 + 15)

**Separation:** how fast the gap opens after. Same idea.

steps.prompt: X at 20 m s⁻¹ chases Y at 12 m s⁻¹ (same direction). What is their speed of approach?
steps.explain: Same direction → subtract: 20 − 12 = **8 m s⁻¹**.
steps.hint: Same direction: subtract.

steps.prompt: Two balls move towards each other at 5 m s⁻¹ and 15 m s⁻¹. Speed of approach?
steps.explain: Towards each other → add: 5 + 15 = **20 m s⁻¹**.
steps.hint: Towards each other: add.

steps.prompt: Elastic collision. Before: X at 20 m s⁻¹, Y at 12 m s⁻¹, both to the right. After: X at 10 m s⁻¹ right, Y at v right. What is v?
steps.explain:
Approach = 20 − 12 = 8.
Separation = v − 10.
Elastic: v − 10 = 8 → **v = 18 m s⁻¹**.

No masses needed!
steps.alt: Before: X 20 m/s and Y 12 m/s to the right. After: X 10 m/s and Y v to the right
steps.hint: Approach speed = separation speed.

steps.prompt: Two bodies on the same line have a perfectly elastic collision. Which statement **must** be correct?
choices: The initial speed of one equals the final speed of the other.
The relative speed of approach equals their relative speed of separation.
Momentum is conserved but total KE is reduced.
One body will be stationary at one instant.
steps.explain: That's the elastic rule. A and D only happen in special cases. C describes inelastic.

steps.prompt: Identical spheres. X moves at v towards stationary Y. The collision is elastic. What happens?
choices: X: ½v right; Y: ½v right
X: v left; Y stays still
X: ½v left; Y: ½v right
steps.explain:
Equal masses, elastic, one at rest → they **swap velocities**.
Check: momentum mv = 0 + mv ✓. Separation v − 0 = v = approach ✓.

A conserves momentum but loses KE, so it isn't elastic.
steps.alt: Sphere X moving right at v towards stationary sphere Y
steps.hint: Equal masses, elastic, one at rest.

steps.prompt: X (5 m s⁻¹ right) and Y (15 m s⁻¹ left) have a perfectly elastic head-on collision. Y then moves right at 7 m s⁻¹. Speed and direction of X?
steps.explain:
Approach = 5 + 15 = 20.
Y is at +7 after. Separation = 7 − v_X = 20 → v_X = −13.
**13 m s⁻¹ to the left.**
steps.alt: Ball X moving right at 5 m/s, ball Y moving left at 15 m/s
steps.hint: Approach = 5 + 15. Y is now going right.

steps.prompt: Spheres approach each other at u₁ (right) and u₂ (left). After a perfectly elastic collision they move right at v₁ and v₂ (v₂ in front). Which must be correct?
steps.explain:
Towards each other → approach = u₁ + u₂.
Same direction after → separation = v₂ − v₁.
So **u₁ + u₂ = v₂ − v₁**.
steps.alt: Before: u1 right and u2 left. After: v1 and v2 both right
steps.hint: Towards each other before, same direction after.

steps.prompt: Elastic collision: X (mass m) at v hits stationary Y (mass 4m). X rebounds at 3v/5. What is the kinetic energy of Y after?
steps.explain:
Momentum: mv = m(−3v/5) + 4mV
4V = v + 3v/5 = 8v/5 → V = 2v/5
KE = ½ × 4m × (2v/5)² = 2m × 4v²/25 = 8mv²/25 = **16/50 mv²**.

Check with the shortcut: separation = 2v/5 + 3v/5 = v = approach ✓.
steps.alt: X mass m at v hits stationary Y mass 4m. After: X moves left at 3v/5, Y moves right
steps.hint: Use momentum to find Y's speed, then ½mv².

steps.prompt: If the speed of separation is less than the speed of approach, the collision is inelastic.
steps.explain: Smaller separation speed means some KE was lost → inelastic.

steps.prompt: A 0.50 kg ball at 6.0 m s⁻¹ makes a perfectly elastic head-on collision with a stationary 1.0 kg ball. Find both velocities after the collision. [4]
steps.solution:
Right = +. Let after velocities be v₁ (0.50 kg) and v₂ (1.0 kg).

**Momentum:** 0.50 × 6.0 = 0.50v₁ + 1.0v₂
→ 3.0 = 0.50v₁ + v₂ (1)

**Elastic:** approach = separation
6.0 = v₂ − v₁ → v₂ = v₁ + 6.0 (2)

Sub (2) into (1): 3.0 = 0.50v₁ + v₁ + 6.0
1.5v₁ = −3.0 → v₁ = −2.0
v₂ = 4.0

**Answer: 0.50 kg ball: 2.0 m s⁻¹ backwards (left). 1.0 kg ball: 4.0 m s⁻¹ forwards.**

Check KE: before ½(0.5)(36) = 9.0 J; after ½(0.5)(4) + ½(1)(16) = 1 + 8 = 9.0 J ✓
steps.hint: Write a momentum equation and an approach = separation equation.

steps.title: Split into x and y
steps.text:
Momentum is a vector, so in 2D:

**x-momentum is conserved on its own.**
**y-momentum is conserved on its own.**

Use components: p cos θ and p sin θ.

steps.title: Sticking together at an angle
steps.text:
Find total pₓ and total p_y.

Angle: **tan θ = p_y ÷ pₓ**
Size: **p = √(pₓ² + p_y²)**

steps.prompt: A 0.20 kg ball moving in the x-direction at 0.50 m s⁻¹ hits a 0.30 kg ball moving in the y-direction at 0.40 m s⁻¹. They stick. Angle θ to the x-direction?
steps.alt: 0.20 kg ball moving in x-direction at 0.50 m/s and 0.30 kg ball moving in y-direction at 0.40 m/s
steps.hint: tan θ = p_y ÷ pₓ. Use momenta, not velocities.

steps.prompt: Same collision: what is the speed of the combined 0.50 kg lump?
steps.hint: p = √(pₓ² + p_y²), then divide by the total mass.

steps.title: Sideways momentum must cancel
steps.text:
A moving nucleus hits a stationary one. Before, there's **no sideways (y) momentum**.

After, the two paths must have sideways momenta that cancel: **one goes up, one goes down**. If both go to the same side, it's impossible.

steps.prompt: A nucleus collides with a stationary nucleus in a vacuum. Which diagram is **not** possible?
steps.explain:
No sideways momentum before → after, one particle must go up and one down.
In **C**, both particles go downward → total y-momentum isn't zero → impossible.

steps.prompt:
A ball of mass m at u hits a stationary ball M. After: m moves at v, 30° above the line; M moves at V, 40° below. Which equations are correct?
(1) mu = MV + mv
(2) mv sin 30° = MV sin 40°
(3) mu = mv cos 30° + MV cos 40°
steps.explain:
(1) ✗ — you can't just add vectors at angles.
(2) ✓ — sideways: up momentum = down momentum.
(3) ✓ — along the line: the cos components add up to mu.
steps.alt: Ball m at u hits stationary M. After, m goes 30 degrees above, M goes 40 degrees below
steps.hint: Check each direction separately: along the line and sideways.

steps.prompt: A 2.0 kg puck at 5.0 m s⁻¹ (x-direction) hits a stationary 2.0 kg puck. Afterwards the first puck moves at 3.0 m s⁻¹ at 53° above x. Find the y-component of velocity of the second puck (size).
steps.explain:
y before = 0.
First puck: p_y = 2.0 × 3.0 × sin 53° = 2.0 × 2.40 = 4.79
Second puck: 2.0 × v_y = 4.79 (downwards)
v_y = **2.4 m s⁻¹**.
steps.hint: Sideways momentum before is zero.

steps.title: Traps to watch for
steps.text:
• g vs kg, ms vs s, kN vs N — **convert first**
• Bounce → **add** the speeds
• Opposite directions → one velocity is **negative**
• Momentum is a vector, KE is a scalar
• 'Elastic' → you can use approach = separation

steps.prompt: In an inelastic collision, total energy is not conserved.
steps.explain: **Total** energy is always conserved. Only **kinetic** energy is lost (it becomes thermal energy, sound, etc.). Saying 'energy is lost' instead of 'kinetic energy is lost' can cost a mark.

steps.prompt: In which of these is momentum conserved? (No external forces.)
steps.explain: **All of them.** Momentum is always conserved in an isolated system. Only KE differs.

steps.prompt: A ball falls and hits the ground. Why isn't momentum conserved for the ball on its own?
choices: Gravity and the ground exert external forces on it
steps.explain: Conservation needs **no resultant external force**. The system 'ball + Earth' conserves momentum; the ball alone doesn't.

steps.prompt: Which quantity has the same unit as momentum?
steps.explain:
Impulse = F × t, unit N s = kg m s⁻¹.
F × d = J; ma = N; E/t = W.

steps.prompt: Base units of momentum?
steps.explain: p = mv → kg × m s⁻¹ = **kg m s⁻¹**.

steps.prompt: Two trolleys at rest are pushed apart by a spring. The 0.60 kg trolley moves off at 0.50 m s⁻¹. The other moves at 0.75 m s⁻¹. What is its mass?
steps.explain:
Starts at 0 → equal and opposite momenta.
0.60 × 0.50 = 0.30 = m × 0.75
m = 0.30 ÷ 0.75 = **0.40 kg**.
steps.hint: It starts at rest, so the momenta are equal and opposite.

steps.prompt: A 0.40 kg ball and a 0.60 kg ball have equal kinetic energies. Which has the larger momentum?
steps.explain:
p = √(2mEₖ). Same Eₖ → bigger m gives bigger p.
The **0.60 kg** ball.

steps.prompt: An object has Eₖ = 50 J and momentum 10 kg m s⁻¹. What is its mass?
steps.explain:
Eₖ = p² ÷ 2m → m = p² ÷ 2Eₖ = 100 ÷ 100 = **1.0 kg**.

(Useful: Eₖ = p²/2m.)
steps.hint: Eₖ = p² ÷ 2m

steps.prompt: A force–time graph is a rectangle 4.0 N high and 0.50 s wide, acting on a 2.0 kg object at rest. Final speed?
When you jump, the Earth gains momentum equal and opposite to yours.
steps.explain: Total momentum is conserved. The Earth's mass is huge, so its velocity change is tiny.

steps.prompt:
A 1200 kg car at 15 m s⁻¹ hits the back of a stationary 1800 kg van. They lock together.
(a) Find their speed just after. [2]
(b) Find the kinetic energy lost. [3]
(c) Explain why total energy is still conserved. [1]
steps.solution:
**(a)** Momentum: 1200 × 15 = (1200 + 1800)v
18 000 = 3000v → **v = 6.0 m s⁻¹**

**(b)** KE before = ½ × 1200 × 15² = 135 000 J
KE after = ½ × 3000 × 6.0² = 54 000 J
Lost = **81 000 J (81 kJ)**

**(c)** The lost kinetic energy is transferred to other forms (thermal energy, sound, and work done deforming the metal). The total energy stays the same.
steps.hint: (a) momentum; (b) ½mv² before and after.

steps.prompt:
A trolley A (0.80 kg) moves at 0.60 m s⁻¹ towards a stationary trolley B (0.40 kg). After the collision, A moves at 0.20 m s⁻¹ in the same direction.
(a) Find the velocity of B. [2]
(b) Use relative speeds to decide if the collision is elastic. [2]
steps.hint: Momentum for (a). For (b), compare approach and separation.

steps.prompt:
A ball of mass 0.30 kg is thrown at a wall at 12 m s⁻¹ and rebounds at 9.0 m s⁻¹. It is in contact for 0.050 s.
(a) Calculate the change in momentum. [2]
(b) Calculate the average force on the ball. [1]
(c) State the size and direction of the average force on the wall, and name the law. [2]
steps.solution:
**(a)** Towards wall = +.
Δp = 0.30 × (−9.0) − 0.30 × 12 = −2.7 − 3.6 = **−6.3 kg m s⁻¹** (6.3, away from the wall)

**(b)** F = 6.3 ÷ 0.050 = **126 N ≈ 130 N** (away from the wall)

**(c)** **126 N towards the wall** — Newton's **third law** (equal and opposite forces between the ball and the wall).
steps.hint: Take towards the wall as +. The rebound velocity is negative.

steps.title: Why reps?
steps.text:
Hard momentum questions are mostly easy physics plus **algebra**: converting units, signs, solving two equations, sin/cos and areas.

Get these automatic and the hard questions get way easier.

steps.prompt: Convert 250 g to kg.
Convert 72 km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹.
steps.hint: Divide by 3.6.

steps.prompt: 3.5 ms = 3.5 × 10ⁿ s. What is n?
Right is positive. A ball moves left at 5 m s⁻¹. Its velocity is:
steps.explain: Left = negative: **−5 m s⁻¹**.

steps.title: Two equations, two unknowns
steps.text:
Elastic problems give you two equations:
(1) momentum
(2) approach = separation

Make one unknown the subject of (2), then **substitute** it into (1).

steps.prompt: Solve: 2v₁ + 3v₂ = 12 and v₂ − v₁ = 4. What is v₂?
steps.explain:
From (2): v₂ = v₁ + 4.
Sub in: 2v₁ + 3v₁ + 12 = 12 → 5v₁ = 0 → v₁ = 0.
**v₂ = 4**.
steps.hint: Write v₂ = v₁ + 4 and substitute.

steps.prompt: Solve: v₁ + 2v₂ = 6 and v₂ − v₁ = 3. What is v₁?
steps.hint: Substitute v₂ = v₁ + 3.

steps.title: Components
steps.text:
A vector of size A at angle θ to the x-axis:

**x-part = A cos θ**
**y-part = A sin θ**

Calculator in **degrees** mode!

steps.prompt: A puck moves at 10 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the x-axis. x-component of velocity?
steps.hint: Adjacent side → cos.

steps.prompt: Momentum 6.0 kg m s⁻¹ at 40° below the x-axis. Size of the y-component?
steps.hint: Opposite side → sin.

steps.title: Areas under graphs
steps.text:
Triangle: **½ × base × height**
Rectangle: **base × height**
Trapezium: split into a triangle + rectangle + triangle.

steps.prompt: Find the area under this force–time graph (the impulse).
steps.explain:
Rise: ½ × 2 × 8 = 8
Flat: 3 × 8 = 24
Fall: ½ × 1 × 8 = 4
Total = **36 N s**.
steps.hint: Split it into two triangles and a rectangle.
steps.alt: Force rises from 0 to 8 N over 2 s, stays at 8 N until 5 s, falls to 0 at 6 s

steps.prompt: Solve ½ × 3.0 × v² = 24 for v.
steps.hint: Divide by 1.5 first, then square-root.

steps.prompt: p = 6.0 kg m s⁻¹ and m = 2.0 kg. Use Eₖ = p² ÷ 2m to find Eₖ.
Speed of an object dropped from 1.8 m just before it hits the floor? (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
steps.hint: mgh = ½mv² → v = √(2gh)

steps.title: Two graph facts
steps.text:
**Gradient of a p–t graph = resultant force**

**Area under an F–t graph = impulse = Δp**

Those two ideas answer almost every momentum-graph question.

steps.prompt: What resultant force acts from t = 0 to 4 s?
steps.hint: Rise ÷ run.
steps.alt: Momentum rises in a straight line from 2 at 0 s to 14 at 4 s, then stays flat

steps.prompt: Same graph: what is the resultant force after t = 4 s?
steps.explain: Flat line → gradient 0 → **no resultant force**. It keeps moving at constant velocity.
steps.alt: Momentum rises in a straight line, then is flat after 4 s

steps.prompt: The momentum of a car changes as shown. What is happening to the resultant force?
choices: It is zero all the time
steps.explain: The curve gets **less steep**. Gradient = force, so the force **decreases** (like air resistance growing as the car speeds up).
steps.alt: Momentum rises quickly at first, then the curve levels off

steps.prompt: The force shown acts on a 1.5 kg object that starts at rest. Final speed?
steps.hint: Area under the graph = Δp.
steps.alt: Force rises to 8 N at 2 s, flat to 5 s, falls to 0 at 6 s

steps.title: Reading a v–t graph of a collision
steps.text:
Before the jump = before the collision.
After the jump = after.

Read each velocity off the graph, then use **p = mv** for each trolley.

steps.prompt: Trolley A (0.50 kg) hits stationary trolley B (1.5 kg). What is B's speed after? (Check it with momentum.)
steps.explain:
Before: 0.50 × 4 = 2.0.
After: 0.50 × 1 + 1.5v = 2.0 → v = **1.0 m s⁻¹**. Matches the graph.
steps.hint: Total p before = total p after.
steps.alt: A at 4 m/s until 2 s then 1 m/s; B at 0 then 1 m/s

steps.prompt: The collision in that graph is elastic.
steps.explain:
After, both move at 1 m s⁻¹, so the separation speed is 0 but the approach speed was 4. They stuck together, so it's **inelastic**.
KE: before 4.0 J, after 1.0 J.
steps.alt: Both trolleys move at 1 m/s after the collision

steps.prompt: A 0.15 kg ball hits a bat at 12 m s⁻¹. The graph shows the force on it. What is the ball's speed as it leaves, in the opposite direction?
steps.explain:
Impulse = ½ × 10 ms × 600 N = ½ × 0.010 × 600 = 3.0 N s.
Take the return direction as +: Δp = 0.15v − 0.15(−12) = 3.0
0.15v + 1.8 = 3.0 → v = **8.0 m s⁻¹**.
steps.hint: Area first (ms → s). Then Δp = m(v + 12).
steps.alt: Force rises from 0 at 1 ms to 600 N at 6 ms, back to 0 at 11 ms

steps.prompt: Graphs X and Y show the force during two landings of the same jumper. Which is true?
choices: X gives the bigger change in momentum
Both give the same change in momentum, but X has a bigger peak force
Y has the bigger peak force
Both have the same peak force
steps.explain:
Areas: X = ½ × 0.1 × 200 = 10 N s; Y = ½ × 0.4 × 50 = 10 N s. **Same Δp.**
X lasts a shorter time, so it needs a much bigger force. That's why bending your knees (Y) hurts less.
steps.hint: Compare the areas, then the heights.
steps.alt: X: tall narrow triangle peaking at 200 N over 0.1 s. Y: low wide triangle peaking at 50 N over 0.4 s

steps.prompt: Sketch the momentum–time graph for a ball dropped from rest that hits the floor and bounces back up (take downwards as +). Describe each part. [3]
steps.solution:
**Falling:** p increases in a straight line from 0 (constant gradient = weight mg).

**Bounce:** p drops very steeply from +p₁ to a negative value −p₂ in a very short time (a big force from the floor).

**Rising:** p goes from −p₂ back towards 0 in a straight line with the **same gradient** as the fall (gravity is still the only force).

|p₂| < |p₁| if some KE is lost in the bounce.

steps.title: Two-stage problems
steps.text:
Some problems have a **collision** and then **motion**.

Collision → use **momentum** (KE usually isn't conserved).
Motion before or after → use **energy** (KE ↔ GPE) or SUVAT.

Never use KE conservation across a sticky collision.

steps.prompt: Ballistic pendulum: after the hit, the block and bullet (2.02 kg) swing up 0.10 m. Their speed just after the hit? (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
steps.hint: KE after the hit turns into GPE at the top.
steps.alt: A 0.020 kg bullet flies into a 2.0 kg block hanging on strings; the block swings up 0.10 m

steps.prompt: Same pendulum: what was the bullet's speed?
steps.hint: Now use momentum for the hit.
steps.alt: Ballistic pendulum diagram

steps.prompt: Same pendulum: what percentage of the bullet's KE was lost in the hit?
steps.explain:
KE before = ½ × 0.020 × 141.4² ≈ 200 J
KE after = ½ × 2.02 × 1.4² ≈ 1.98 J
Lost ≈ 198 J → **≈ 99 %**.
That's why you can't use KE conservation for the hit!
steps.hint: Compare ½mv² just before and just after the hit.

steps.title: Bounces with gravity
steps.text:
Ball dropped → hits floor → bounces up.

1. Speed in: v = √(2gh₁)
2. Speed out: v = √(2gh₂)
3. Δp = m(v_in + v_out)
4. Net force = Δp ÷ t
5. Floor force = net force **+ weight** (the floor has to hold the ball up too).

steps.prompt: A 0.50 kg ball falls from 1.8 m and bounces to 0.80 m. Size of its change in momentum during the bounce? (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
steps.hint: Find both speeds with v = √(2gh).

steps.prompt: Same ball: contact lasts 0.050 s. What is the average force from the floor?
steps.explain:
Net force = 4.95 ÷ 0.050 = 99 N (upwards).
Net = floor force − weight → floor force = 99 + 0.50 × 9.8 = **104 N**.
99 N is the trap: that's the resultant force, not the floor's force.
steps.hint: Net force = floor force − weight.

steps.title: Spring explosions
steps.text:
Trolleys pushed apart by a spring:
• Momentum: m₁v₁ = m₂v₂ (start at rest)
• Energy: spring energy = ½m₁v₁² + ½m₂v₂²

Use momentum to link v₁ and v₂, then the energy equation.

steps.prompt: A spring storing 1.2 J pushes apart a 0.40 kg trolley and a 0.60 kg trolley at rest. Speed of the 0.60 kg trolley?
steps.hint: Write v₁ in terms of v₂ using momentum, then put it into the energy equation.

steps.prompt: The lorry (20 000 kg, 20.0 m s⁻¹) and car (900 kg, 30.0 m s⁻¹ towards it) lock together. Their speed just after?
steps.hint: Use the total momentum from before, divided by the total mass.
steps.alt: Lorry moving right at 20 m/s, car moving left at 30 m/s

steps.prompt: A 1.0 kg ball at 4.0 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary 3.0 kg ball. The collision is perfectly elastic. Speed of the 3.0 kg ball afterwards?
steps.explain:
Momentum: 4.0 = v₁ + 3v₂
Elastic: 4.0 = v₂ − v₁ → v₁ = v₂ − 4
4 = v₂ − 4 + 3v₂ → 4v₂ = 8 → **v₂ = 2.0 m s⁻¹**
(v₁ = −2.0: the light ball bounces back.)
steps.hint: Two equations: momentum and approach = separation.

steps.prompt: Same collision: what happens to the 1.0 kg ball?
choices: It bounces back at 2.0 m s⁻¹
steps.explain:
v₁ = v₂ − 4 = 2 − 4 = **−2.0 m s⁻¹**: it bounces back.
A light ball hitting a heavy one elastically always bounces back.

steps.prompt: A neutron (mass m) hits a stationary carbon nucleus (mass 12m) head-on, elastically. What fraction of its KE does the neutron keep?
steps.explain:
For a light ball hitting a stationary heavy one elastically: v_after = (m − 12m)/(m + 12m) × u = −(11/13)u.
KE ∝ v², so the fraction kept is **(11/13)² ≈ 0.72**.
steps.hint: Use momentum + relative speed with masses m and 12m. Then KE ∝ v².

steps.title: How to score on structured questions
steps.text:
• Write the **equation** first, then substitute, then the answer **with units**.
• State a **direction** for vectors.
• For 'show that', show every line.
• For definitions, use the exact Cambridge wording.

steps.prompt:
A puck of mass 0.30 kg moving at 4.0 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary puck of mass 0.20 kg. After the collision, the 0.30 kg puck moves at 2.0 m s⁻¹ at 30° to its original direction, as shown.
(a) Calculate the x- and y-components of the 0.20 kg puck's velocity. [3]
(b) Find its speed and direction. [2]
(c) Determine whether the collision is elastic. [2]
steps.hint: Do x and y separately. Before the hit, the y-momentum is zero.
steps.alt: 0.30 kg puck at 4.0 m/s hits stationary 0.20 kg puck; afterwards the 0.30 kg puck goes at 2.0 m/s, 30 degrees above, and the 0.20 kg puck goes below the line

steps.prompt: A stationary nucleus of mass 222u emits an α-particle (4u) at 1.5 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. Recoil speed of the remaining 218u nucleus?
steps.explain:
Starts at rest → 4 × 1.5 × 10⁷ = 218 × v
v = 6.0 × 10⁷ ÷ 218 = **2.75 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹**.
(The u units cancel, so you don't need kg.)
steps.hint: Total momentum before is zero.

steps.prompt: Same decay: how many times bigger is the α-particle's KE than the recoiling nucleus's KE?
steps.explain:
Same size p for both, and Eₖ = p² ÷ 2m, so Eₖ ∝ 1/m.
Ratio = 218 ÷ 4 = **54.5**.
steps.hint: Eₖ = p²/2m with the same p.

steps.prompt: Water leaves a hose nozzle of area 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² at 15 m s⁻¹ and hits a wall without bouncing. Density of water = 1000 kg m⁻³. Force on the wall?
steps.hint: Mass per second = density × area × speed.

steps.prompt:
(a) State the principle of conservation of momentum. [2]
(b) A 60 kg astronaut floating at rest throws a 2.0 kg tool at 6.0 m s⁻¹. Calculate the astronaut's recoil velocity. [2]
(c) Calculate the total kinetic energy produced and state where it came from. [2]
steps.solution:
**(a)** The total momentum of a system remains constant, provided no resultant external force acts on it.

**(b)** 0 = 2.0 × 6.0 + 60v → **v = −0.20 m s⁻¹** (0.20 m s⁻¹, opposite to the tool)

**(c)** KE = ½ × 2.0 × 6.0² + ½ × 60 × 0.20² = 36 + 1.2 = **37.2 J**
It came from the **chemical energy** in the astronaut's muscles.
steps.hint: Total momentum before the throw is zero.

steps.prompt:
A 0.40 kg trolley P moves at 3.0 m s⁻¹ and collides with a 0.60 kg trolley Q moving at 1.0 m s⁻¹ in the same direction. After the collision, Q moves at 2.6 m s⁻¹.
(a) Calculate P's velocity after. [2]
(b) Show that the collision is elastic using relative speeds. [2]
(c) Calculate the average force on Q if the collision lasts 0.12 s. [2]
steps.hint: Momentum for (a); approach vs separation for (b); F = Δp/Δt for (c).

steps.prompt: Which is a correct statement of Newton's second law?
choices: The resultant force is proportional to the rate of change of momentum
Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
Momentum is constant if no force acts
steps.explain: That's the Cambridge wording. C is Newton's 3rd law; D is about conservation (or the 1st law).
steps.skill: Force = rate of change of momentum

steps.prompt: Which is the correct definition of linear momentum?
steps.explain: Momentum = mass × **velocity** (a vector).

steps.prompt: A 0.50 kg ball hits a wall at 8.0 m s⁻¹ and rebounds at 6.0 m s⁻¹. Contact time 0.020 s. Average force?
steps.explain:
Δp = 0.50 × (8.0 + 6.0) = 7.0 N s.
F = 7.0 ÷ 0.020 = **350 N**.
50 N is the 'subtract the speeds' trap.
steps.skill: Force = rate of change of momentum
steps.hint: It bounced, so add the speeds.

steps.prompt: Which row is correct for a perfectly elastic collision in an isolated system?
steps.explain: Elastic → KE conserved. Isolated → momentum always conserved.

steps.prompt: A 3.0 kg ball at 4.0 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary 1.0 kg ball. They stick together. Common speed?
steps.hint: They move together after.

steps.prompt: A 70 kg skater at rest pushes a 50 kg skater, who moves off at 1.4 m s⁻¹. Speed of the 70 kg skater?
steps.hint: Starts at rest: equal and opposite momenta.

steps.prompt: A force on a 2.0 kg mass falls steadily from 6.0 N to 0 in 4.0 s. The mass starts at rest. Final speed?
steps.skill: Force = rate of change of momentum
steps.hint: Area of the triangle = impulse.

steps.prompt: Elastic collision. P moves right at 9 m s⁻¹, Q moves left at 3 m s⁻¹. Afterwards Q moves right at 6 m s⁻¹. Velocity of P after?
steps.explain:
Approach = 9 + 3 = 12.
Separation: 6 − v_P = 12 → v_P = −6 → **6 m s⁻¹ left**.
steps.hint: Approach = 9 + 3.

steps.prompt: In an inelastic collision, the total momentum after is less than before.
steps.explain: Momentum is always conserved (isolated system). Only KE decreases.

steps.prompt: A machine gun fires 10 bullets per second, each of mass 0.020 kg, at 500 m s⁻¹. Average force on the gun?
steps.hint: Momentum given to bullets each second.

steps.prompt: A 0.10 kg ball moves at 3.0 m s⁻¹ in the x-direction and hits a stationary ball. After, the first ball moves at 90° to its original path. Which must be true about the second ball?
choices: It moves along the x-direction only
Its x-momentum is 0.30 kg m s⁻¹
steps.explain:
First ball now has no x-momentum (it moves at 90°).
So the second ball carries all the x-momentum: 0.10 × 3.0 = **0.30 kg m s⁻¹**. It also needs y-momentum to cancel the first ball's, so A is wrong.
steps.hint: The second ball must carry all the x-momentum.

steps.prompt: The area under a force–time graph equals the change in ___.
steps.explain: Area = F × t = impulse = **change in momentum**.
steps.skill: Force = rate of change of momentum

steps.prompt: A 2.0 kg object moving at 6.0 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary 4.0 kg object and they stick. Kinetic energy lost?
steps.explain:
v = 12 ÷ 6.0 = 2.0 m s⁻¹.
KE before = ½ × 2.0 × 36 = 36 J
KE after = ½ × 6.0 × 4 = 12 J
Lost = **24 J**.
steps.hint: Find the common speed first.

steps.prompt: Which unit is equivalent to N s?
steps.explain: N s = kg m s⁻² × s = **kg m s⁻¹**.

steps.prompt: A ball bounces off a wall elastically. Which are true?
choices: Its speed is the same after
The wall exerts a force on it
steps.explain: Direction reverses → momentum changes. Elastic → same speed and same KE. The wall provides the force that changes the momentum.

steps.prompt: A 5.0 kg shell at rest explodes into 2.0 kg and 3.0 kg pieces. The 2.0 kg piece moves at 30 m s⁻¹. Total kinetic energy released?
steps.hint: Find the 3.0 kg piece's speed from momentum first.

steps.prompt: Why does a long jumper land in a sand pit?
choices: To reduce the change in momentum
To increase the stopping time, so the force is smaller
steps.explain: Δp is the same either way. F = Δp/Δt: longer time → smaller force.
steps.skill: Force = rate of change of momentum

steps.prompt: Two identical trucks: one at rest, one moving at v. They collide elastically head-on. Afterwards:
choices: the moving one stops; the other moves at v
the moving one bounces back at v
steps.explain: Equal masses, elastic, one at rest → velocities swap.

steps.prompt: A 900 kg car at 20 m s⁻¹ brakes to rest in 4.5 s. Average braking force (size)?
steps.skill: Force = rate of change of momentum
steps.hint: F = Δp ÷ t

steps.prompt:
(a) Define impulse. [1]
(b) A 0.058 kg tennis ball arrives at 25 m s⁻¹ and leaves the racket at 35 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. Contact time is 4.0 ms. Find the average force on the ball. [3]
(c) State whether the collision is elastic. Explain. [1]
steps.solution:
**(a)** Impulse = force × time for which it acts (= change in momentum).

**(b)** Δp = 0.058 × (35 + 25) = 0.058 × 60 = 3.48 N s
F = 3.48 ÷ 0.0040 = **870 N**

**(c)** **Not elastic for the ball alone** — it leaves faster than it arrived, so it gained KE from the racket (the racket does work on it). An external force (the player) acts on the system, so you can't treat it as an isolated elastic collision.
steps.skill: Force = rate of change of momentum
steps.hint: Bounce: add the speeds. 4.0 ms = 0.0040 s.

steps.prompt:
A 2.0 kg trolley X at 3.0 m s⁻¹ makes a perfectly elastic collision with a stationary 1.0 kg trolley Y.
(a) Write the momentum equation. [1]
(b) Write the relative-speed equation. [1]
(c) Find both velocities after. [2]
(d) Show that KE is conserved. [2]
steps.hint: Momentum equation + relative speed equation, then solve them together.
